result.question:
I have a feeling we keep fixing the same fault on Transformer 1 at site MAIN without ever getting to the root cause. Check that for me.

Pull all closed work orders on Transformer 1 with their number, description, completion date and failure code. Use our failure code catalog to map each one to a transformer fault type: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core or winding thermal fault, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation.

Then work out what the transformer is doing now. Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and use co from the same sample to check whether the paper is involved. Map that result to the same list of fault types.

Call it a recurring fault only if at least two closed work orders map to the same fault type the gases show today.

If it's recurring:
- Check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing root cause investigation or manufacturer referral. If there is one, give me its number and don't duplicate it.
- Otherwise, create a priority 2 root cause investigation work order. List the earlier work order numbers in the notes, add a note to notify the manufacturer, and code it with the matching failure code.

If only one earlier job matches, don't create anything. Recommend a confirmatory oil resample and say that one repeat isn't enough to call a pattern. If none match, say today's fault looks new.

If a closed work order has no failure code, map it from its description and mark it as inferred. Inferred matches can support a recurrence but can't be the only basis for one. If the latest sample is missing any of the five gases, use the most recent complete sample and give its timestamp.
result.answer:
I've completed the check. Here's the result.

**Closed work orders on Transformer 1 (MAIN)**

| WO | Description | Completed | Failure Code | Mapped fault type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000052 | Transformer 1 oil sample retest and insulation check – DGA thermal fault (Rogers T3 hot metal) | 2026-09-30 | FC006 (overheating or high temperature reading) | Core or winding thermal fault (high-temperature T3, hot metal) |

That is the only closed work order on this asset. WO 1000051 (OLTC inspection, tap changer wear/coking) is still open (APPR), not closed, so it can't support a recurrence count.

**Current gas signature — latest complete sample (2024-01-18T00:00:00)**

- H2 2900, CH4 7350, C2H6 5450, C2H4 16600, C2H2 7 ppm (all five gases present; sample is complete)
- Rogers ratios: r1 = CH4/H2 = 2.53 (code 1), r2 = C2H4/C2H6 = 3.05 (code 2), r3 = C2H2/C2H4 = 0.0004 (code 0)
- Classification: **high-temperature thermal fault (T3, >700 °C, hot metal)** → maps to **core or winding thermal fault**
- CO from the same sample: 33 ppm — low and stable across the window, so the **paper/cellulose is not involved**; this is a hot-metal (core/lamination/connection) thermal fault, not cellulose ageing.

**Verdict: NOT a recurring fault**

Only one closed work order (1000052) maps to the core/winding thermal fault the gases show today — that's one match, not the two required for a recurrence. Note also that the earlier WO actually concluded the DGA had "settled" and was stable, and today's sample is essentially unchanged from it.

No new work order created. My recommendation instead:

- Take a **confirmatory oil resample** in the near term to verify the T3 signature is still stable rather than trending.
- One repeat isn't enough to call a pattern — if a future resample again classifies as T3 hot metal, that plus WO 1000052 would meet the recurrence threshold and would warrant a priority 2 root cause investigation.

One caveat: the DGA interpretation tool was unavailable (repeated LLM errors), so the classification above was computed manually from the IEC 60599 Rogers ratio method using the sample values — the result (r1>1, r2>3, r3<0.1 → T3 high-temperature thermal fault) is unambiguous, but it's worth re-running through the tooling when it's back online.
